p: A sum/sum-of-squares approach gives O(1) extra space with algebra: sum difference and square-sum difference give the two numbers. The Counter version is simpler and easier to explain, at O(n²) extra space for the n² values.

p: source `abcd`, target `acbe`, rules a→b (2), b→c (5), c→b (5), c→e (1), e→b (2), d→e (20) → 28. Rule strings are numbered `{'a': 0, 'b': 1, 'c': 2, 'e': 3, 'd': 4}` and the cheapest conversions found by Floyd–Warshall include b→c = 5, c→b = 3, d→e = 20. DP over positions:

Changing `x` into `y` may use a chain of rules, so the cost between two strings is a shortest path: Floyd–Warshall computes it for all pairs of rule strings. The positions of the actual string are then handled by a prefix DP: at position i we either skip an equal letter or replace a block of one of the allowed lengths. The problem guarantees replaced blocks don't partially overlap, so non-overlapping blocks left to right is enough.

bullets: Time: O(k³ + n · (number of distinct lengths) · L) for k rule strings.

2977.takeaway: Floyd–Warshall for the cheapest conversion between rule strings, then a left-to-right DP over positions choosing block lengths.

blocks.h: Why is the frequency bound enough?
p: Each part must contain distinct elements, so a value can appear at most once in each of the two parts, i.e. at most twice overall. If every value appears at most twice, put one copy of each repeated value in each part and fill the rest evenly: both parts have n/2 distinct elements (the lengths work out because the total is even).

p: Lexicographic order is decided by the earliest position where strings differ, so make the first letter as small as possible, then the second, and so on. Making a letter 'a' costs its circular distance; spending budget earlier (left) always beats saving it for later letters. When the budget can't reach 'a', use it all to reduce this letter as much as possible, going backwards.

3106.takeaway: Greedy left to right: turn each letter into 'a' if the circular distance fits the budget, otherwise move it back as far as the leftover budget allows.

Every entry is a power of two, so a product of entries is 2^(sum of their exponents). Define `pre(k)` = sum of exponents of the first k entries; the answer is 2^(pre(r+1) − pre(l)) mod m. To get `pre(k)` without building the array (indexes go up to 10¹⁵), find the largest n whose numbers 1…n contribute at most k entries (binary search using bit counting), add all their exponents with a closed formula, and finish the partial number n+1 bit by bit. The closed formulas agree with a brute-force product on the five queries above: True.

3145.takeaway: Products of powers of two are 2^(exponent sums): count entries and exponents in 1…n with bit-counting formulas and binary search for the cut.

blocks.h: Why does the total score collapse to end − start?
p: Each move scores destination − source, so along a path the intermediate values cancel (telescoping sum): the score is just the final value minus the starting value. The best path to a cell therefore starts at the smallest cell that can reach it (anything above and to the left). Tracking that minimum per cell gives the answer in one pass. The path must contain at least one move, so a cell's own value is not used as `prev` for itself: `mn` is updated AFTER computing the candidate.

bullets: Space: O(m·n) (O(n) with a rolling row).

3148.takeaway: Moves telescope: score = end − start, so for each cell subtract the smallest value above-left and take the maximum.

p: The challengers face the champion in index order the first time around, and a defeated champion goes to the back (behind everyone not yet seen). The DP matches a brute-force enumeration of all permutations on five small cases (including different requirement sets for n = 3 and 4): True.

blocks.h: Why inserting elements one by one?
p: Build a permutation by placing the i-th element into the arrangement of the first i−1 elements (as relative ranks). Putting it at position p creates exactly i − p new inversions with the earlier elements, which is any number from 0 to i. So the inversion counts of prefixes evolve with a sliding-window sum, and a requirement on a prefix is a filter on that DP array.

bullets: Time: O(n · M) with prefix sums.

3193.takeaway: Insertion DP over inversion counts: dp'[j] = sum of dp[j−i … j]; apply each prefix requirement as a filter.

p: `[1,2,3,4,5]`, `k = 2` → 5. For each target `s`, `dp[r]` after processing all numbers:

The condition says every neighbouring sum has the same remainder s. For a fixed s, each new element x can follow an element with remainder (s − x) mod k, so only the last remainder matters, giving a k-state DP. Trying all s from 0 to k−1 covers every possible common remainder, at O(k · n) total.

3202.takeaway: For each common sum-remainder s run a DP keyed by the remainder of the last element: x can follow a subsequence ending with remainder (s − x) mod k.
